metadata.description:
Case name: United States v. Nordic Village, Inc.

Opinion filed: 1992-02-25

Docket No.: 90-1629

Citations:
• 117 L. Ed. 2d 181
• 112 S. Ct. 1011
• 503 U.S. 30
• 1992 U.S. LEXIS 1371

Case holding summaries:
• it is a "settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such a fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• providing as an example the "‘sweeping language’ of the Federal Tort Claims Act" (cita- tions omitted)
• “[T]he Government’s consent to be sued must be construed strictly in favor of the sovereign.” (internal quotations omitted)
• “Waivers of the Government’s sovereign immunity, to be effective, must be unequivocally expressed.” (internal quotations omitted)
• noting “the settled rule that a statute 19 must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect”
• noting the “settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative ef- fect”
• noting the "settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be con- strued in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• applying a similar rule of construction where a was “susceptible of at least two interpretations,” one of which was more intrusive on a state’s interests
• "As in the Eleventh Amendment context, the `unequivocal expression' of elimination of sovereign immunity that we insist upon is an expression of statutory text."
• declining to adopt a construction that would violate the "settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• stating that a waiver of sovereign immunity “must be construed strictly in favor of the sovereign” and “not enlarge[d] . . . beyond what the language requires” (in- ternal quotation marks omitted)
• "settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• statutes must "be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• holding that the existence of “plausible” interpretations that would not permit recovery “is enough to establish that a reading imposing monetary liability on the Government is not ‘unambiguous’ and therefore should not be adopted”
• construing an ambiguous waiver of sovereign immunity to permit equitable but not monetary claims
• "[T]he Government's consent to be sued must be `construed strictly in favor of the sovereign,' and not 'enlarged ... beyond what the language requires.'" (citations omitted)
• for waiver of sovereign immunity, "[i]f clarity does not exist [in the text], it cannot be supplied by a committee report"
• such clauses are broad waivers of immunity
• noting the “settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be con- strued in such fashion that every word has some operative effect”
• “[T]he Government’s consent to be sued must be construed strictly in favor of the sovereign . . . and not enlarged . . . beyond what the language requires . . .” (citation and internal quotations omitted)
• the sovereign immunity of the United States is not "liberally construed"
• explaining that every word must be given operative effect otherwise one paragraph in the statute would have no function
• "[T]he `unequivocal expression' of elimination of sovereign immunity that we insist upon is an expression in the statutory text. If clarity does not exist there, it cannot be supplied by a committee report."
• waivers of sovereign immunity by the United States government must be "unequivocally expressed"
• relying on sovereign immunity principles to construe statutory waiver of sovereign immunity to permit equitable but not monetary claims
• stating that it is a "settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• "[It is a] settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such a fashion that every word has some operative effect."
• federal jurisdiction did not exist where respondent sought to recover sum of money rather than "particular dollars" in a segregated or identifiable fund
• "a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• It is a "settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such a fashion that every word has some operative effect."
• "a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• "the Government's consent to be sued must be construed strictly in favor of the sovereign and not enlarge[d] ... beyond what the language requires."
• applying a similar rule of construction where a was “susceptible of at least two interpretations,” one of which was more intrusive on a state’s interests
• "[W]e have never applied an in rem exception to the sovereign-immunity bar against monetary recovery, and have suggested no such exception exists. . . ."
• "a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• holding that "a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• court must construe government's consent to be sued strictly in favor of the sovereign
• "As in the Eleventh Amendment context, the 'unequivocal expression' of elimination of sovereign immunity that we insist upon is an expression of statutory text."
• observing "[w]e have on occasion narrowly construed exceptions to waivers of sovereign immunity where that was consistent with Congress' clear intent, as in the context of the `sweeping language' of the [FTCA]" (quoting Yellow Cab Co., supra, at 547)
• It is a settled rule “that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect.”
• "A suit for payment of funds from the Treasury is quite different from a suit for the return of tangible property in which the debtor retained ownership"
• discussing immunity of United States
• recognizing that a provision of the bankruptcy code waived sovereign immunity from monetary claims in two settings but declining to find such a waiver in a third setting
• holding sovereign immunity presumptions applicable in Bankruptcy Court
• “[A] statute must, if possible, be construed in such a fashion that every word has some operative effect.”
• noting in dicta that the predecessor to § 106(b) waives the sovereign immunity of the United States with respect to "compulsory counterclaims to governmental claims"
• interpreting 11 U.S.C. § 106(c)
• old § 106(c) did not waive the sovereign immunity of the United States for an action seeking a monetary recovery in bankruptcy because there was not "an unequivocal textual waiver"
• declining to adopt a construction that would violate the "settled rule that a statute must, if possible, be construed in such fashion that every word has some operative effect"
• "Waivers of the Government's sovereign immunity, to be effective, must be `unequivocally expressed.'"
